description:
A long conversation about one question. How accurately can we predict how many primes there are up to a number x? Gauss found a smooth average in 1795, and Riemann showed in 1859 that the error of that average is set by where the zeros of the zeta function lie. The Riemann Hypothesis says they all lie on the line with real part ½. In autumn 2026 an AI produced a formally verified proof of a weaker statement, which keeps the zeros away from the edge of the strip and gives a smaller error bound than anything proved before.

This is the podcast edition of the explainer video Predicting Primes. It walks through the same chain at a slower pace, from primes through Euler's product and the zeta function to the zeros and the error, with short excerpts from the interview.

Chapters
0:00 September 30, 2026
3:37 What is a prime?
7:21 Has AI solved the Riemann Hypothesis?
8:48 Gauss and the density of primes
13:58 π(x), Li(x) and the error
17:43 The zeta function
21:16 Euler's product
25:00 The pole at s = 1
28:10 The prime counter and the waves from the zeros
33:27 The map and analytic continuation
37:21 The chain from primes to the error
37:57 Where the zeros sit sets the error
41:34 The Riemann Hypothesis
44:14 A trillion and half the digits
48:03 1896 and the century after
51:18 The AI result of 2026
54:07 How the AI did it and how Lean checks it
56:47 Recap

Interview excerpts come from the World Science Festival video "AI Closes In on the Riemann Hypothesis", in which Brian Greene talks with Alex Kontorovich (https://youtu.be/ljFZfYZLHj8). They are used for commentary and education, and all rights remain with World Science Festival.

The conversation was made with NotebookLM from an original script.
